blocks.text: Once the ASC certified product leaves the ownership of the farm UoC, each subsequent company in the supply chain that owns ASC certified product must hold valid ASC Chain of Custody certification. This assures consumers and seafood buyers that ASC labelled products come from certified farms. ASC uses the Marine Stewardship Council’s (MSC) Chain of Custody (CoC) Standard, plus the ASC-owned CoC Module, to verify the origin of seafood sold as ASC certified. This process benefits companies that handle both ASC and MSC certified seafood by allowing them to do a combined audit. CoC certification covers activities beyond farm production, such as processing and packing. For more information see Chain of Custody Standard – ASC International or contact info@asc-aqua.org.

blocks.text: The independent actors and processes described above are interlinked to provide the most robust and reliable assurance system, supported by ASC’s transparent processes and stakeholder participation. The CABs conduct strict audits to verify conformity against the ASC standards. ASI assesses the CABs to confirm that certification was granted following the requirements and with integrity. Both CABs and ASI may conduct these activities unannounced, and all the evaluation results are publicly available for interested stakeholders who may provide additional information to the certification process.

blocks.text: The impacts of aquaculture extend beyond the final grow-out site, as the supply chain for many species involves multiple production stages across different sites. A major challenge in addressing these impacts is the diversity of practices found both between and within species production and the sharing of information between various sites. Addressing these impacts and enabling the supply chain to carry batch-specific information is essential to ensuring that the industry operates responsibly as a whole.

blocks.text: The aquaculture industry is ideally positioned to help provide the food needed to support a growing global population due to its smaller environmental footprint than many land-based animal sources. Maintaining this advantage requires ongoing stewardship of the environmental impacts. Through the initiatives outlined in this principle, ASC supports the industry to develop in an environmentally responsible manner to meet this challenge.

blocks.text: Aquaculture relies on ecosystems to provide resources, including water, as well as the absorption of its outputs, including waste from farm processes, to operate1111Gephart, J. A., Henriksson, P. J., Parker, R. W., Shepon, A., Gorospe, K. D., Bergman, K., … & Troell, M. (2021). Environmental performance of blue foods. Nature, 597(7876), 360-365.. Without proper management, the environment’s capacity to keep providing these resources and assuming these outputs can be exceeded, leading to concerns about biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions that drive climate change, and inefficient resource use.

blocks.text: Aquaculture farms affect nearby habitats and species through both siting and operational activities. Choosing farm sites carefully is crucial to protect ecologically sensitive areas and managing farm practices is equally important. This includes managing benthic impacts, controlling nutrient release into open waters, reducing wildlife conflict, and preventing farmed animals from escaping and affecting native biodiversity. Addressing these challenges is key to tackling global biodiversity loss1313Aguilar-Manjarrez, J., Soto, D., & Brummett, R. (2017) Aquaculture zoning, site selection and area management under the ecosystem approach to aquaculture. A handbook. Rome, Italy: FAO..

Understanding the likelihood of negative impacts occurring from an activity, and the magnitude of that impact, requires a risk-based approach. An Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) is a useful tool to help identify the risks of environmental risks associated with an activity along with actions to help mitigate those risks.

blocks.text: Aquaculture production can drive conversion and fragmentation of ecologically important habitats if improperly sited. Farms sited in protected or sensitive habitats can affect local biodiversity and the ecological services these environments provide.Loss of wetlands has been historically linked to expansion of aquaculture in tropical regions. blocks.text: Aquaculture operations may result in human-wildlife interactions and conflict in many ways. Farms may rely on wildlife directly for collection of larvae, juveniles, or breeding stock. Their vessels, infrastructure, or equipment may disturb or interact with wildlife. They may also use deterrent devices to discourage predators or pests from approaching pens or cages. Risk to wildlife from these interactions should be assessed and mitigated and, when injuries or mortalities do occur, corrective measures need to be put into place to avoid similar future occurrences.

blocks.text: The introduction of non-native (or alien) species, often driven by human activities, poses significant concerns for natural ecosystems. Their impacts can vary widely, from negligible effects to severe ecological disruptions. These consequences often emerge after extended periods and can vary significantly based on the biological traits of the species and the characteristics of the receiving ecosystem.2323Blackburn , T. M., Essl, F., Evans, T., Hulme, P. E., Jeschke, J. M., Kühn, I., … & Bacher, S. (2014). A unified classification of alien species based on the magnitude of their environmental impacts. PLoS biology, 12(5), e1001850. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001850

blocks.text: The global aquaculture industry is a key contributor to the spread of alien species. Many of these species have escaped into the wild, establishing populations that can cause ecological harm. This underscores the need for effective management strategies and scientifically sound evaluation tools.

blocks.text: To address these challenges, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) developed the Environmental Impact Classification for Alien Taxa2424International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). (2020). IUCN EICAT Categories and Criteria. The Environmental Impact Classification for Alien Taxa. Gland, Switzerland and Cambridge, UK: IUCN. https://doi.org/10.2305/IUCN.CH.2020.05.en (EICAT). EICAT assesses potential impact mechanisms and categorises impacts into specific levels. This framework helps prioritise management efforts by identifying harmful species, ensuring resources are allocated effectively, and addressing knowledge gaps for species with insufficient data.

blocks.text: The benthic zone (‘bottom’) of a waterbody often supports a rich biodiversity and provides critical ecological functions such as assimilation of organic material (e.g. faeces, uneaten feed), provision of food for native species and protection of coastal sediment from erosion. Human activities interacting with the benthic zone can negatively impact the functioning of these ecosystems.

blocks.text: Aquaculture can interact with the benthic zone through deposition of organic material and release of heavy metals.2525González-Gaya, B., García-Bueno, N., Buelow, E., Marin, A., & Rico, A. (2022). Effects of aquaculture waste feeds and antibiotics on marine benthic ecosystems in the Mediterranean Sea. Science of the Total Environment, 806, 151190. When this deposition exceeds the environment’s ability to handle it, harmful changes to the ecosystem can occur.2626Hargrave, B. T., Phillips, G. A., Doucette, L. I., White, M. J., Milligan, T. G., Wildish, D. J., & Cranston, R. E. (1997). Assessing benthic impacts of organic enrichment from marine aquaculture. In The Interactions Between Sediments and Water: Proceedings of the 7th International Symposium, Baveno, Italy 22–25 September 1996 (pp. 641-650). Springer Netherlands. The severity of these impacts depends on factors such as the amount of waste released, water body characteristics and the ability of the benthic microbial community to break down waste.2727Kalantzi, I., & Karakassis, I. (2006). Benthic impacts of fish farming: meta-analysis of community and geochemical data. Marine Pollution Bulletin, 52(5), 484-493.

blocks.text: Salinisation occurs when salt concentration rises in soil or freshwater, either naturally or due to human activities. With a growing global population, addressing salinisation is crucial for food security.3636Kumar, P., & Sharma, P. K. (2020). Soil salinity and food security in India. Frontiers in sustainable food systems, 4, 533781.

blocks.text: Freshwater is a vitally important global resource. As a result of increasing demand, water scarcity is increasing, leading to regional ‘water stress’. The source of fresh water, the local conditions, and the intensity of extraction determine whether the utilisation of resources is detrimental to the natural environment and to humans. Global freshwater resource depletion is driven primarily by food production systems.4040Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). (2022). The State of the World’s Land and Water Resources for Food and Agriculture 2021—Systems at a Breaking Point. Rome, Italy: FAO. https://doi.org/10.4060/cb9910en

blocks.text: From construction, to operation and decommissioning, aquaculture farms use materials and generate waste that can be hazardous. Copper-based antifoulants can leach into the water and cause harm to marine life in the water column and to the sediments below the farm. Therapeutants and chemicals used to treat farmed animals can also create unintended impacts on the animals themselves, the ecosystem and their handling staff.

blocks.text: All children have the right to be protected from work that is dangerous or harmful to their health, development or education.5959International Labour Organization (ILO). (1999). Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention, 1999 (No. 182). Geneva, Switzerland: ILO.6060International Labour Organization (ILO). (1973). Minimum Age Convention, 1973 (No. 138). Geneva, Switzerland: ILO. Employment and exploitation of children and young workers occurs globally across many sectors and is driven by economic and cultural pressures on the poorest, most vulnerable people.6161International Labour Office and United Nations Children’s Fund. (2021). Child labour: Global estimates 2020, trends and the road forward. New York, USA: ILO and UNICEF However, limited and non-harmful forms of participation in the workforce can contribute to a child’s development in some contexts, providing them with skills for their adult life and supporting the welfare of their families.

blocks.text: This Criterion focuses on the prevention of child labour and the provision of safe working conditions for young employees on ASC certified farms. Rather than disengaging from any abuses identified, as part of ASC’s approach to respect human rights and work on improvements in aquaculture, this Criterion requires that effective remediation is conducted.

blocks.text: An estimated 22 million people are employed worldwide in aquaculture production.6464Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). (2024). The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024—Blue transformation in action. Rome, Italy: FAO. https://doi.org/10.4060/cd0683en These workers regularly contend with hazardous conditions and suffer injuries relating to the use of machinery, tools, boats, vehicles, drowning, falling and electrocution. The risks of accidents or incidents typically remain unaddressed due to gaps in knowledge, limited independent analyses of prevention measures or a lack of investment in risk reduction strategies. With adequate health and safety management, many of these incidents can be prevented and additional costs can be avoided.

blocks.text: Employment contracts consist of terms and conditions that address aspects of the employment such as the respective responsibilities of employer and employee. They are designed to give both parties clarity, trust, assurance and protection, through clear and understandable explanation of the obligations for both sides. If these agreements are not clearly understood by the employee, confusion and disagreements may result. Contracting employees in a transparent manner increases accountability in the workplace, helping to build a positive relationship between employer and employee. This Criterion focuses on employers committing to, and employees clearly understanding the terms and conditions of, their employment – contributing to transparency and accountability on ASC certified farms.

blocks.text: Every employee deserves to be fairly compensated for their efforts. In many countries, this compensation is insufficient to maintain a decent standard of living, leaving employees and their families in a cycle of poverty which is difficult to escape from. Across many industries, efforts are being made to progress compensation up to the level of a living wage, defined as “the remuneration received for a standard workweek by a worker in a particular place sufficient to afford a decent standard of living for the worker and her or his family. Elements of a decent standard of living include food, water, housing, education, health care, transportation, clothing, and other essential needs including provision for unexpected event.”6565https://www.globallivingwage.org/about/what-is-a-living-wage/

Although these interventions are intended to benefit both parties, there is a risk that this could be done in an unfair or degrading manner towards the employee.

blocks.text: Aquaculture sites are often located in remote areas, including off-shore operations. Daily commutes between shifts are usually difficult under these circumstances, and as a result, employees may reside for a duration in accommodation provided by their employer. In certain regions and particular industries, employees might decide to live with their families on the site. Where employee accommodation is provided, there can be a risk that the living conditions are poor, with limited freedom of movement or access to sanitary facilities – posing a physical and mental health risk. Poor accommodation is strongly linked to forced labour.7272International Labour Organization (ILO). (1961). Workers’ Housing Recommendation, 1961 (No. 115). Geneva, Switzerland: ILO.

blocks.text: Grievance mechanisms may be referred to as dispute, complaint or accountability mechanisms. They offer a system in which parties can effectively address a problem together, provide remediation where needed and serve as an early warning system for human rights issues to inform corrective actions. They also offer the right to external redress. Well-functioning grievance mechanisms are transparent, fair, predictable, accessible to all stakeholder groups and foster trust among participants.7373United Nations. (2011). Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. Implementing the United Nations “Protect, Respect and Remedy” Framework. Human Rights Office of the High Commissioner.

Through this commitment, ASC also addresses a spectrum of global challenges, including food security, ecosystem resilience, global warming and threats to public health. By recognising the connection between these issues, animal health and welfare in aquaculture emerges as a critical focus, providing a holistic approach to safeguarding people, animals and the environment.

blocks.text: The ASC Farm Standard adopts a comprehensive framework for animal health and welfare that encompasses ethical, economic, environmental, and regulatory considerations to mitigate risks, and prevents poor animal health and welfare outcomes.

blocks.text: ASC embraces a definition of welfare defined by the physical and mental state of an animal in relation to the conditions in which it lives and its capacity to cope with the environment providing opportunities for animals to ‘thrive’ and not simply survive. This perspective is linked to the concept of Positive Animal Welfare (PAW), which can be characterised by four features: positive emotions, positive affective engagement, quality of life and happiness. These features extend the original Five Freedoms7575Green, T., & Mellor, D. (2011). Extending ideas about animal welfare assessment to include ‘quality of life’ and related concepts. New Zealand Veterinary Journal, 59(6), 263–271. https://doi.org/10.1080/00480169.2011.610283,7676Mellor, D. J. (2016). Updating Animal Welfare Thinking: Moving beyond the “Five Freedoms” towards “A Life Worth Living”. Animals, 6(3), 21. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani6030021 to incorporate consideration of quality of life.

blocks.text: Many animals, including fish, are sentient beings that can feel and experience pain, stress and anxiety. Keeping them in good health and welfare is a responsible practice that support animals to adapt to their surroundings, boosts productivity, prevents the spread of disease and reduces reliance on chemicals with potentially negative environmental effects. Handling activities and slaughter are major factors in the welfare of farmed animals. If not carried out appropriately, they can lead to stress and overall suffering.7777Ashley, P. J. (2007). Fish welfare: current issues in aquaculture. Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 104(3-4), 199-235.

blocks.text: Maintaining good health and welfare in aquaculture production includes consideration of a wide range of practices and conditions. Key aspects include disease detection and response, feeding practices, appropriate handling of animals and monitoring of water conditions.7777Ashley, P. J. (2007). Fish welfare: current issues in aquaculture. Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 104(3-4), 199-235. Best practices in fish slaughter include the implementation of responsible stunning and killing methods to ensure that there is rapid loss of consciousness, which is not regained before killing.7878Lines, J. A., & Spence, J. (2014). Humane harvesting and slaughter of farmed fish. Revue scientifique et technique (International Office of Epizootics), 33(1), 255-264. An effective management plan and site-specific handling plans can help avoid mortality events, demonstrating commitment to responsible aquaculture practices.

blocks.text: Many animals are sentient beings that can feel and experience pain, stress and anxiety. While the question of the sentience of crustaceans is still being discussed, keeping them in good health and welfare is a responsible practice that supports them to adapt to their surroundings, boosts productivity, prevents the spread of disease and reduces reliance on chemicals with potentially negative environmental effects. Handling activities and slaughter are major factors in the welfare of farmed animals. If not carried out appropriately, they can lead to stress and overall suffering.8888Pedrazzani, A. S., Cozer, N., Quintiliano, M. H., Tavares, C. P. d. S., da Silva, U. d. A. T., & Ostrensky, A. (2023). Non-Invasive Methods for Assessing the Welfare of Farmed White-Leg Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei). Animals, 13(5), 807. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani13050807

blocks.text: Maintaining good health and welfare in aquaculture production includes consideration of a wide range of practices and conditions.7777Ashley, P. J. (2007). Fish welfare: current issues in aquaculture. Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 104(3-4), 199-235. Key aspects include disease detection and response, feeding practices, appropriate handling of animals and monitoring of water conditions. Best practices in the slaughter of crustaceans include the implementation of responsible stunning and killing methods to ensure that there is rapid loss of consciousness, which is not regained before killing.8989Pedrazzani, A. S., Cozer, N., Quintiliano, M. H., Tavares, C. P. d. S., da Silva, U. d. A. T., & Ostrensky, A. (2023). An effective management plan and site-specific handling plans can help avoid mortality events, demonstrating commitment to responsible aquaculture practices.

blocks.text: A Risk Management Framework is a structured method used to assess and control risks in a systematic and consistent manner. It helps to understand how likely and severe a risk is so that steps can be taken to reduce or prevent it. Conducting risk assessments helps individuals and companies in the aquaculture industry become aware of risks and improve operational processes. The main steps involve identifying risks, assessing the risk level, implementing control measures, monitoring, regularly reviewing and updating the assessment to ensure its effectiveness.

blocks.text: As filter-feeders, bivalves depend on the natural abundance of phytoplankton for feeding. In situations where bivalve aquaculture exceeds the ability of the waterbody to provide for sufficient phytoplankton for both natural bivalve populations and cultured populations, the carrying capacity can be exceeded and depletion can occur. Within this Appendix, various calculations are provided to determine if phytoplankton depletion occurs within a waterbody.

blocks.text: For cage culture and suspended marine mollusc culture systems (Indicators 2.5.1 and 2.5.2), the ASC method for benthic monitoring requires sampling at predefined zones to determine benthic status. The method is based on a three-level approach in which a site conducts increasingly more detailed benthic monitoring if the results of Level 1 or Level 2 monitoring do not demonstrate an ‘Acceptable’ benthic status. Conversely, a site that demonstrates an ‘Acceptable’ benthic status in Level 1 or Level 2 does not need to conduct a higher level of monitoring. Sites may decide to start monitoring at any of the three levels. The method uses five benthic Ecological Quality Status (EQS) categories that are numerically defined using a range of abiotic and biotic indicator thresholds (see Table 1 and Table 2). An EQS Category is assigned to the monitoring results of each sampling zone  which determines the benthic status of a site.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(5)

html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(57)

blocks.text: Sediment sampling for macrofauna taxonomic analysis shall be conducted yearly in the receiving river in at least three transects 10 metres apart,  upstream and downstream from the site outflow point. Each transect shall contain at least four sampling locations for a minimum of 24 samples.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: The sampling shall focus on key sensitive indicator species for the region.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(1) > ul:nth-of-type(1) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: The transects shall be located to include sampling locations midstream, near the bank and in areas with slower water flow.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(1) > ul:nth-of-type(1) > li:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: The sampling locations shall include areas with similar conditions, such as bottom type, water flow and/or substrate types, along the bank in the upstream and downstream sampling locations.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(1) > ul:nth-of-type(1) > li:nth-of-type(3)

blocks.text: The position of the sampling locations downstream shall reflect a scientific assessment of the most likely area of potential impact from the site, considering the mixing of water and the minimum and maximum distance from the site outflow point.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(1) > ul:nth-of-type(1) > li:nth-of-type(4)

blocks.text: The samples shall be analysed to determine the presence, composition, abundance and diversity of invertebrate benthic fauna.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: With the results of the analysis of the samples, the benthic status for the upstream and downstream sampling locations shall be determined using a categorisation system that includes at least five categories of benthic status.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(3)

blocks.text: The determined category downstream shall be compared with the category upstream to demonstrate that the benthic status of the river does not deteriorate downstream from the site’s outflow point.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(12) > li:nth-of-type(4)

blocks.text: In case the downstream sampling locations drop in benthic status category, two sediment sampling for macrofauna taxonomic analysis shall be conducted during the next 12-month period following the method outlined in this section and using the previously used categorisation system.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(58)

blocks.text: After three years of demonstrating conformance with Indicator 2.5.4, sites may reduce sampling to once per certification cycle (i.e. every three years) as long as there have been no significant changes to farming practices and thus that previously determined benthic status provides a credible proxy for future performance.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(59)

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(6)

blocks.text: Sediment sampling shall be conducted in duplicate in three of the transects required by the Level 2 monitoring sampling method for Cages in Marine/Brackish Waters outlined in Section 7.2.1.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(13) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: Of the three transects, one should be upstream and one downstream with respect to the direction of the predominant current.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(13) > li:nth-of-type(1) > ul:nth-of-type(1) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: In each transect, samples shall be collected in Zone 2 and at the reference site outlined in Figure 1.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(13) > li:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: The samples shall be analysed for copper levels expressed in mg Cu/kg dry sediment weight, and the result compared with the metric required by Indicator 2.11.11.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(13) > li:nth-of-type(3)

blocks.text: Sampling shall be conducted at the same time as per the timing required by the benthic sampling method for cages in marine/brackish waters outlined in Section 7.2.1.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(13) > li:nth-of-type(4)

blocks.text: 7.7 Methods for Field Analysis of Abiotic Indicators (Indicator 2.5.1)

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(7)

blocks.text: The method is described and assessed in Cranford (2024)106106Cranford, P. J. (2024). A simple and rapid method for measuring total free sulfides in marine sediments. Limnology and Oceanography: Methods. https://doi.org/10.1002/lom3.10619 and is listed as a recognised,  validated method in the US National Environmental Methods Index (listed as “A simple and rapid method for measuring total free sulfides in marine sediments107107National Environmental Methods Index”). This field method includes the extraction and analysis of porewater in surficial sediments collected by core or grab samplers.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(61)

html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(62)

blocks.text: Drain water in the sediment sampler to the sediment surface.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: Three Rhizon tubes are inserted into the sediment between the undisturbed surface and 2cm depth. Note that a 5cm long Rhizon is inserted at an angle to sample within the 0–2 cm depth range.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: Flush each tube by withdrawing 0.5–1.0mL of porewater into each syringe. Discard the flushing water inside the syringe.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(3)

blocks.text: A 100-µL sample of porewater is immediately removed from inside each Rhizon tube by inserting the needle attached to a 100-µL gas-tight syringe. An extension tube or adapter may be necessary between the Rhizon and syringe to hold sufficient sample volume.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(4)

blocks.text: The 100-µL sample is immediately added to a 1.4mL capacity semi-micro quartz cuvette (1cm pathlength) along with 1mL of deionised water having a pH of approximately 8. The pH of this alkaline dilution water is previously adjusted with ammonium hydroxide and confirmed with pH-indicator strips.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(5)

blocks.text: The 100-µL sample is immediately added to a 1.4mL capacity semi-micro quartz cuvette (1cm pathlength) along with 1mL of deionised water having a pH of approximately 8. The pH of this alkaline dilution water is previously adjusted with ammonium hydroxide and confirmed with pH-indicator strips.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(6)

blocks.text: Immediately place the cuvette into a mobile UV spectrophotometer and measure light absorption at 230, 240 and 250nm wavelengths. The instrument is to be frequently blanked with a cuvette containing the alkaline dilution water.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(7)

blocks.text: Calculate the total free sulfide concentration using the absorbance values and the regression equations determined by the calibration procedure below. Although absorption data are collected for three wavelengths, S2- is only calculated using the lowest wavelength that provides absorbance readings below 2. If the absorbance reading at 230nm is >2, then use the 240nm absorbance, etc.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(14) > li:nth-of-type(8)

html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(63)

blocks.text: The calibration of the UV spectrophotometer is highly stable and only needs to be conducted once a month to ensure the instrument has not been damaged. A concentrated Certified Reference Material (CRM) or Reference Standard is used as the stock solution for preparing five working standards of known sulfide concentration between 0 and 15,000µM.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(64)

blocks.text: Dilute the stock CRM solution to prepare five known concentrations using pipettors and the alkaline deionised water.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(15) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: Blank (zero) the instrument and then add 100µL of the working standard to the cuvette along with 1mL of alkaline water. Record the light absorbance of each working standard at 230, 240 and 250nm wavelengths.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ol:nth-of-type(15) > li:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: Calculate the calibration equations for each of the three wavelengths using regression analysis (x= absorbance at selected wavelength and y= working standard concentration in µM units) while excluding any absorbance readings above 2.

blocks.text: Prior to field measurements, prepare the Sulfide Anti-Oxidant Buffer (SAOB). Dissolve 20.0g NaOH (sodium hydroxide) crystals in 250ml of de-aerated deionised water (use a volumetric type flask). Add 17.9g EDTA (ethylene diamine tetra acetic acid disodium salt dehydrate) to NaOH solution and swirl until dissolved. Place solution in plastic screw top jar. Larger volumes can be prepared as necessary provided ratio of reagents is maintained. Add L-ascorbic acid just prior to analysis of samples. Store in the dark at 4°C. De-aerated deionised water must be at a similar temperature as that of the sediment to be sampled. The SOAB expiration period is 3 hours.

blocks.text: The tip of the electrode should be gently cleaned using an abrasive strip or detergent solution before each calibration. If difficulty is experienced in obtaining the expected slope for the relationship between mV potential and log sulfide concentrations cleaning may be necessary to remove coatings formed on the electrode tip.

blocks.text: In order to measure S2–ISE a 1:1 volume ratio of SAOB to sediment is required. Place 10 mL of SAOB in a small plastic or glass graduated container and then add surface sediment (0 – 2cm depth) until the meniscus is at the 20mL gradation (always add SAOB first).

blocks.text: Briefly stir the mixture and then insert the Ag+/S= electrode into the sample. Ensure the tip of the electrode is fully covered by the SAOB/sediment slurry. Gently move the electrode in the slurry until the electrode stabilises. Depending on the electrode, a ‘Ready’ message appears on the meter screen and/or a beep is heard (typically requiring 1 – 4 minutes to stabilise).

blocks.text: If potentials recorded with the Ag+/S= electrode in a sediment sample do not stabilise in 1 – 2 minutes, performance can be assessed by determining the S2-ISE concentration in one of the working standards that has been stored in a dark cooled container with a minimum head space. Do not attempt to correct the data for drift if deviations are less than 10 – 20% of expected standard values. If measured values have a greater deviation than the expected value a full recalibration should be performed following the calibration protocols.

blocks.text: The following protocols are generic to the Ag+/S= electrode. Specific models may have slightly different specific requirements and the operator must be familiar with the model prior to calibrating the electrode. If routinely used, Ag+/S= combination electrodes should be replaced every couple of years as they tend to become less accurate due to wear and tear.

blocks.text: Working in a fume-hood or well-ventilated area, add 0.2402g Na2S•9H2O to a volumetric flask containing 100 mL of de-aerated deionised water. Swirl until dissolved. Store this 10,000µM stock standard in a refrigerated in dark, air-tight bottle with minimum head space. The stock solution expiration period is two days. Stock standards should be prepared strictly according to Standard Method 4500-S2- (APHA 2017), which provides information on the safe handling and storage of the stock crystals, and the verification of the prepared stock concentration using titration methods (e.g. Iodometric Standard Method 4500-S2--F).

blocks.text: Prepare a serial dilution (10,000μM, 1,000μM, 100μM and 10μM (if required) of S2- standards immediately before calibrating the Ag+/S= combination electrode by transferring 10mL of the 10,000μM Na2S stock solution into a volumetric flask and diluting with 90mL of de-aerated, deionised water. This procedure is repeated sequentially using 10mL of each successive standard and diluting with 90mL of de-aerated,deionised water. The de-aerated, deionised water must be at a similar temperature as that of the sediment to be sampled. The working standard expiration period is 3 hours.

blocks.text: The steps to conduct the sampling of feed lots per site are as follows:

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(27)

blocks.text: The steps to conduct the testing are as follows:

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(31)

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul:nth-of-type(15) > li:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: On-site sampling shall revert to every quarter for another year (12 months) if at least one of the following applies:

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul:nth-of-type(15) > li:nth-of-type(3)

blocks.text: Hydraulic Retention Time shall be determined per site, either by calculating its value or from values derived from secondary data. HRT shall be calculated using the following formula:

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(43)

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul:nth-of-type(16) > li:nth-of-type(1)

blocks.text: 8.7 Components of a Water Quality Monitoring Network (Indicator 2.6.8)

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(6)

blocks.text: The intent of the Water Quality Monitoring Network (WQMN) is to establish a mechanism for collaboration and the sharing of information between aquaculture sites in Type A waterbodies. This will provide the foundation for an Area Management Agreement (AMA) in a future version of the ASC Farm Standard.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(61)

blocks.text: Based on the WUM characterised according to the method outlined in Appendix 8 (8.6), the site shall establish, join a WQMN or present evidence of an area-based approach to manage water quality at a national level.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(8) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(62)

blocks.text: The steps to establish a WQMN per site are as follows:

blocks.text: Outreach shall be conducted to ASC certified sites and non-certified sites belonging to ASC Certificate Holders within the defined WUM. This will determine the members of the WQMN.

blocks.text: Each series of steps below details the method for calculating emissions associated with one or more inputs. In each case, emissions are divided by net live weight production, being the harvested weight plus any change in biomass minus input of juvenile inputs (excluding those transferred from other grow-out sites in the case of salmon). Values per tonne of live weight are then entered into the ASC GHG Data Submission Template which facilitates conversion to kg CO2e emissions per kg of edible weight. The ASC GHG Calculator can be used for all steps to assist in calculating and reporting.

blocks.text: Remediation is the process of restoring an individual after a human rights violation has been discovered, reported and verified. The issue can be discovered in several ways, including through the grievance process, internally at a site or during a third-party audit. The United Nations Guiding Principles for Business and Human Rights (UNGPs)115115https://www.business-humanrights.org/en/big-issues/governing-business-human-rights/un-guiding-principles/ require that both states and businesses take steps to ensure that when there are human rights violations, employees have access to effective remedy.

blocks.text: Once a case has been detected, the first step in remediation is for the site to ensure the person’s safety, and make sure that the person does not feel threatened. Not all situations require immediate safeguarding. However, child labour and forced labour often require immediate actions to protect the person and remove them from an unsafe situation until the remediation plan is developed and enacted.

blocks.text: The next step is to develop and agree upon a remediation plan for the person, seeking input from the affected person, as well as external experts when appropriate. When it is a case of child labour, the child’s family or guardian shall also be involved in the process. When the family is not available, local child protection authorities shall be engaged.

blocks.text: Remediation will take different forms depending on the situation and the needs of the person in question but always considers the best interest of the person. The development and implementation of most plans shall involve working with an NGO or other partner organisation and/or government agencies who are experts in the issue. The criminal justice system is contacted when criminal actions have occurred. How quickly the plan is finalised is dependent on the complexity of actions that need to occur and the urgency of the case, but in any case, within 28 calendar days of an abuse finding.

blocks.text: 10.4 Step 3: Implementation and monitoring of remediation plan

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(10) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(4)

blocks.text: Once the plan has been agreed on by all parties, it is implemented and monitored. Major remediation actions shall be completed within three months of finding the abuse. However, in some cases of child labour, implementation of the child’s remediation plan can take up to several years until a child has finished schooling and is eligible for legal employment. In this case, the plan shall be underway (e.g. the child is enrolled in school and the family is supported) at the end of the 90 days, with a clear plan of continued action.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(10) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(18)

blocks.text: Regular monitoring of the plan is important to confirm that the plan is implemented, that the implementation is effective, and that necessary adjustments are made when circumstances change – for example when a child needs to change school enrolment due to a move.

blocks.text: 10.5 Step 4: Corrective action plan to prevent reoccurrence

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(10) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(5)

blocks.text: An effective remediation process includes the development of a corrective action plan to ensure that root causes are understood, and to prevent the abuse from happening again to someone else. To develop this, the UoC shall perform a root cause analysis of what went wrong in their system and shall implement and monitor appropriate corrective actions to prevent recurrence.

blocks.text: Effective sea lice management is essential to protect the health of both farmed and native salmonid populations. An element of management includes setting limits to the number of on-site sea lice to ensure the health and welfare of farmed fish and minimise the risk of sea lice from farmed fish origin affecting native populations, especially during sensitive periods such as the out-migration.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(13) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(2)

blocks.text: Effective management also includes the cooperation of multiple sites within a specific area to manage sea lice collectively. This Area-Based Management approach helps reduce the overall sea lice burden and mitigate the risk of infestation spreading between sites. Key elements of this cooperation include the coordination of activities, such as stocking, treatment and fallowing, and information sharing.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(13) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(3)

blocks.text: Parasiticide treatments are used to reduce the number of sea lice on farmed fish. However, relying heavily on these chemical treatments is not a sustainable long-term solution, as they pose challenges related to environmental impact, the development of resistance, and the health and welfare of the farmed fish. Addressing these challenges requires alternatives to chemical parasiticide treatments aiming to reduce their use and ultimately eliminate reliance on them.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(13) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(24)

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(13) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3:nth-of-type(5)

blocks.text: Indicator 4.5.9 requires that on-site sea lice levels remain below the thresholds outlined in Table 1 during sensitive periods. If thresholds are reached or exceeded, Indicator 4.5.11 requires levels to be reduced within 21 days following the last day of sampling.

source_refs.locator: html:nth-of-type(1) > body:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > main:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > article:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > section:nth-of-type(13) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > p:nth-of-type(27)
